title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai set its transcription service to record meetings on video platforms by default and send the recordings to the company without obtaining explicit consent from all participants. The system captured private work conversations and sensitive information across approximately 25 million users and over 1 billion meetings. A human check at the point of recording, or a requirement to obtain affirmative consent from all meeting participants before any recording began, would have prevented the unauthorized capture.

The company's privacy policy offered users a checkbox to consent to transcript use for AI training, but the lawsuit alleges this mechanism did not adequately inform users that their conversations would be recorded and shared. The deployment failed to distinguish between consent to record and consent to use recordings for model improvement, treating a checkbox opt-in as sufficient permission for a practice that affected non-consenting participants in recorded meetings.

Whether the company's de-identification process actually protects speaker identity and confidential information, and whether the practice violates applicable wiretap laws, are not established by the reporting; they are the subject of ongoing legal claims.

Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed on Friday accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based transcription company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit, brought by California resident Justin Brewer, claims the company's Otter Notebook service records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without notifying all participants that recordings will be shared with Otter to improve its artificial intelligence systems. The lawsuit alleges this practice violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws. Otter has approximately 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since the company's founding in 2016.

The company's privacy policy states it receives explicit permission through a checkbox to use transcripts for AI training purposes, but the lawsuit maintains users are still being deceived about this practice. Recent incidents have highlighted privacy concerns, including cases where confidential business information and sensitive conversations with human rights activists were recorded and shared. The lawsuit challenges Otter's claim that it de-identifies data before feeding it into machine learning systems, arguing the company provides no public explanation of how this process works or whether it truly protects speaker anonymity and confidential information.
